legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting", Shangyin Tan (first author; UC Berkeley) et al. (Zhou, Agrawal, Zhang, Chen, Mang, Lee, Jacob, Sen, Dimakis, Zaharia). arXiv:2610.20563v1 [cs.AI], 14 Oct 2026 (October 2026). Preprint, no venue.
COVERAGE: 14 of 14 pages read, 40,553 of 40,553 chars, including appendices A (tasks) and B (prompts). References were skimmed. Figures are plots only, so I read their captions and axis text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Forgetting is the proposed mechanism. At each round end, discard every agent session and the whole search state (candidate history, scores, feedback) and keep only the best candidate and its score. A fresh agent with an empty context and the same first-turn instructions then starts from that candidate.
  number: none
  setup: team of 4 agents, 3 forgets, so 4 rounds.
  quote: "periodically discarding every agent's session and the candidate history and restarting from the best candidate found so far" (p.2). Also: "We keep only the best candidate because it already contains most of the progress of the previous agent sessions, while the discarded states mainly record how that progress was made." (p.4)
- Single-agent, parallel and team scaling all plateau as session history accumulates. The paper's explanation is that agents become anchored to their own past attempts.
  number: none
  setup: autoresearch loops with a scored verifier.
  quote: "all three strategies eventually plateau as the agents accumulate history. Each agent becomes anchored to its own past attempts, making fewer and smaller edits." (abstract, p.1)
- A team with forgetting beats both baselines on all four tasks.
  number: +10% mean vs 4 parallel agents; +22% vs 1 agent; up to 15% and 39% in the abstract.
  setup: Pi agent with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, same total budget per configuration ($20 to $40 per replicate), 3 runs per task, 4 tasks (AHC014, VLIW kernel, Frontier-CS Q171, nanochat-autoresearch).
  quote: "On average across the four tasks, it improves on the parallel agents by 10% and on a single agent by 22%." (p.6)
  Table 1 (p.6), mean of 3 runs: AHC014 795k / 964k / 1,103k (1 agent / 4 parallel / team with forgetting, higher is better). VLIW cycles 1,426 / 1,220 / 1,097 (lower is better). Q171 64.0 / 70.2 / 80.8. nanochat val BPB 0.980 / 0.980 / 0.961.
  Parallel agents gain nothing on nanochat: "On nanochat-autoresearch they bring no gain at all." (p.6)
- Continue vs forget from the same plateaued state: continuing barely helps and costs more. Forgetting gains more at about half the cost.
  number: continue +1.6% / +1.9% / +1.4%; forget +4.5% / +7.0% / +9.2%; spend $15.32 vs $24.67 for the team.
  setup: AHC014 only, 30 more proposals per agent, 3 replicates, single agent / 4 parallel / team of 4.
  quote: "Forgetting gains 4.5% for the single agent, 7.0% for the parallel agents and 9.2% for the team at little more than half the cost." (p.7)
  Table 3 (p.8): team of 4, start 951,931, Continue +1.4%±1.3% $24.67, Forget +9.2%±6.9% $15.32.
- Most of the gain comes from the first forget, and returns shrink.
  number: AHC014 +11.2%, +4.8%, +1.7% after forgets 1, 2 and 3. 32 of 36 forgets produced a new best within the next round.
  quote: "32 of the 36 forgets lead to a new best candidate within the next round." (p.7). Also: "Most of the gain comes from the first forget." (Table 2 caption, p.6)
- Mechanism: edits and reasoning shrink as the session grows, and forgetting resets both.
  number: edits fall from about 100 lines to a few lines. Reasoning tokens fall to "a third or less" of the initial level. The team's edits fall from about 150 lines to 30, and its reasoning from about 28k tokens to 7k, before the first forget. In the 10 proposals after a forget, median edits are 40 lines vs 6 under continuation, and median reasoning tokens are 9.4k vs 2.9k.
  setup: AHC014 trajectories, 3 replicates pooled (Figure 5), and the same-state experiment (Figure 4).
  quote: "median edits are 40 lines after forgetting versus 6 under continuation, and median reasoning-token usage is 9.4k versus 2.9k." (p.9)
- Long sessions produce empty turns that declare a plateau early, and these burn money.
  number: 532 of 763 completed turns produced no candidate and used 66.2% of spend (range 58.4% to 70.4% across replicates). 531 of the 532 read at most one file and made no edit.
  setup: VLIW, single agent, $40 per replicate, 3 replicates.
  quote: "532 of 763 completed turns produce no candidate, consuming 66.2% of the model spend." (p.8)
  Example: the agent wrote "I've reached the practical limit of this machine configuration" at 1,710 cycles. The same agent later reached 1,644, and the team with forgetting reached 1,077.
- Communication alone does not remove the plateau.
  number: continuing a team's sessions for 30 more proposals per agent gains 1.4%. On Q171 the team leads parallel agents by 13% before its first forget.
  quote: "continuing the sessions of a team with communication for 30 more proposals per agent gains only 1.4%." (p.6)
- Case study: a fresh agent attempted a bold change and borrowed a peer's trick.
  number: VLIW team went 1,212 to 1,201 before the forget, then reached 1,136 on one candidate, and the round ended at 1,114.
  setup: one VLIW team run. This is an anecdote.
  quote: "The combined version reaches 1,136 cycles, the largest single improvement of the round, and the team ends the round at 1,114 cycles." (p.9)

DESIGN DETAILS (useful for the note)
- The state split is search state (every candidate with score and feedback, as commits in a repo) versus session (the messages and reasoning).
- A "reducer" decides what the agent sees as files and which session it continues. Every configuration is a reducer setting.
- Team communication is peers' candidates as commits plus scores, readable from the workspace. There is no orchestrator and no point-to-point messages, so it is "fully asynchronous and token-free".
- Each turn is stateless in effect. The agent edits and ends its session. A separate process scores it and re-invokes it. The agent is told not to evaluate its own change.

LIMITS
- It uses one model (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) and one harness (Pi), with 3 runs per task. Variance is large: the team's Q171 and nanochat standard deviations are visible, and Table 3 gives +9.2%±6.9%.
- All four tasks have a numeric scorer and a bounded optimum, so open-ended discovery without a verifier is untested.
- Gains shrink over rounds. The number of forgets (3) and the schedule are fixed.
- The authors concede that the open questions are "decide when to forget and what to remember" (p.9). Only the best candidate is kept, with no ablation of keeping a summary or notes.
- The mechanism (anchoring to failures) is shown by correlation in edit size and reasoning tokens, plus anecdotes, not by a causal test.
- Parallel agents help little on nanochat, and the baseline comparisons use equal spend, not equal proposals.
- The Table 1 "Best" figures are the best single run, and the team's best on AHC014 (1,145k) differs slightly from the 1,144,695 in Figure 1.

BUILDS ON: autoresearch (Karpathy, 2026); FunSearch (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024); AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025); GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026); Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026). On clean restarts it cites Recovery-Bench (Tan et al., 2025: agents that inherit failed-attempt history solve fewer tasks than those that start clean) and "Parallel environments for agents" (Tan et al., 2026). Related and concurrent: Fork-and-Flush (Cai et al., 2026; resets the context but keeps the workspace), Stateless Language Agents (Zhang et al., 2026), and "The interaction tax" (Ann et al., 2026; communication homogenizes proposals).

CODE: none. Appendix B (p.13-14) gives the per-turn prompt skeleton. The first turn carries the task, status ("Your current candidate is `<id>`, mean score <score>"), peer branch pointers under `.context/peers/branch<i>/`, and the instruction "Improve the candidate, then end the session... Do not evaluate the change yourself". Later turns carry only the status plus a short "# Continue" reminder with TASK.md as the full instructions.

FIGURES (captions)
- Fig 1 (p.1): best score vs dollars on AHC014 and the VLIW kernel. The 1-agent and 4-parallel curves flatten early, and the team's curve jumps after each forget line. This is the best single picture of the claim.
- Fig 2 (p.4): diagram of continuous session vs team with forgetting. It shows what is kept and what is dropped.
- Fig 3 (p.5): harness diagram with the reducer, search state, sessions and judge. Useful for state-management design.
- Fig 4 (p.7): continue vs forget from the same plateaued state.
- Fig 5 (p.8): lines changed and thinking tokens per proposal, falling with session length and resetting at each forget.

NOTE FIT: 05-long-running-loops.md fits well, because this is evidence that long sessions degrade and that a periodic reset keeping one artifact helps. Secondary fits are 08-self-improving-loops.md (the hillclimb and autoresearch loop shape) and 09-failure-modes-and-guardrails.md (the "anchoring" and "empty plateau turn" failure modes). I did not read these notes. The scorekeeper note (03) could cite the "do not self-evaluate, a separate judge scores" instruction.

PROBLEMS: Extraction was clean. Plot axis text is scrambled but the captions are fine. The paper's text contains no embedded instructions. The arXiv ID 2610.20563 and the other 2026 dates and references are as printed and not checked against anything.
